Mauerbach
MOW-ur-bahkh
n. (the Austrian charterhouse of 1314, in the twentieth century the depot of unrestituted looted art)
German Mauer, a wall, and Bach, a brook; the walled stream.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Mauerbach west of Vienna was founded in 1314 by Frederick the Fair and was the principal Carthusian house of Austria until Joseph II dissolved it in 1782. Its later history is extraordinary. After the Second World War the Austrian republic used the buildings as the central depot for works of art looted by the Nazis whose owners could not be traced, and for decades thousands of paintings and objects sat in the former charterhouse while claims went unanswered. International pressure finally produced a 1995 law, and in 1996 the Mauerbach collection was auctioned in Vienna for the benefit of Holocaust survivors. This dictionary records Mauerbach for that long delay and its ending, because restitution is a biblical obligation with a schedule attached. Repentance is proved by giving the thing back, “If the wicked restore the pledge, give again that he had robbed” (Eze 33:15). Zacchaeus volunteers fourfold, “I restore him fourfold” (Luk 19:8). The law fixed the multiple, “he shall restore five oxen for an ox, and four sheep for a sheep” (Exo 22:1), and required the principal plus a fifth, “that he shall restore that which he took violently away” (Lev 6:4).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines restitution as the act of restoring what was taken; to restore as to return to the owner; a pledge as something given as security; plunder as goods taken by force; and amends as compensation for an injury.

expand to see more

RESTITUTION, n. The act of returning or restoring to a person some thing or right of which he has been unjustly deprived; indemnification.

RESTORE, v.t. To return to a former owner; to give back; as, to restore a stolen article; to repair; to make good.

PLEDGE, n. Something given or deposited as security for the performance of an act; a pawn; a gage.

PLUNDER, n. That which is taken from an enemy by force; pillage; prey; spoil; also, that which is taken by theft or fraud.

AMENDS, n. plu. Compensation for an injury; recompense; satisfaction; equivalent.

Key Scripture

Eze 33:15 — "If the wicked restore the pledge, give again that he had robbed, walk in the statutes of life, without committing iniquity; he shall surely live, he shall not die."

Luk 19:8 — "And Zacchaeus stood, and said unto the Lord; Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold."

Exo 22:1 — "If a man shall steal an ox, or a sheep, and kill it, or sell it; he shall restore five oxen for an ox, and four sheep for a sheep."

Lev 6:4 — "Then it shall be, because he hath sinned, and is guilty, that he shall restore that which he took violently away, or the thing which he hath deceitfully gotten, or that which was delivered him to keep, or the lost thing which he found,"

Modern Corruption

Austrian charterhouse of 1314: for decades after 1945 it held looted art whose owners could not be found, auctioned at last in 1996 for survivors.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture makes giving back the evidence of repentance rather than an optional sequel to it. Ezekiel names the restoring of the pledge as the first thing a turned man does, “If the wicked restore the pledge, give again that he had robbed” (Eze 33:15), and Zacchaeus does not wait to be assessed, “I restore him fourfold” (Luk 19:8).

The second thing is that the law set a multiple, which is uncomfortable because it means restitution costs more than the theft gained, “he shall restore five oxen for an ox, and four sheep for a sheep” (Exo 22:1), with the principal and a fifth required in the case of a trust violated, “that he shall restore that which he took violently away” (Lev 6:4). A state that held other people's paintings in a monastery for fifty years while heirs died was not keeping a neutral position. The principle to recover is that delay in restitution is itself a form of keeping.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shub (H7725), to restore; Greek apodidomi (G591), to give back; Hebrew chabol (H2258), a pledge; Hebrew shalam (H7999), to make good; Greek tetraploos (G5073), fourfold.

expand to see more

Hebrew chabol (H2258) — a pledge, to be handed back; “If the wicked restore the pledge”, Ezekiel 33:15.

Hebrew gezelah (H1500) — what was robbed, to be given again; “give again that he had robbed”, Ezekiel 33:15.

Greek tetraploos (G5073) — fourfold, volunteered; “I restore him fourfold”, Luke 19:8.

Hebrew shalam (H7999) — to make whole, to repay; “he shall restore five oxen for an ox”, Exodus 22:1.

Hebrew gazal (H1497) — to take by violence; “that he shall restore that which he took violently away”, Leviticus 6:4.

Usage

"“If the wicked restore the pledge, give again that he had robbed” (Eze 33:15) — restitution as the evidence of repentance."

"“I restore him fourfold” (Luk 19:8) — volunteered, not assessed."

"“he shall restore five oxen for an ox” (Exo 22:1) — it costs more than the theft gained."
